Esophageal Atresia +/- Fistula
Notes

At a Glance: Emergencies by Age

Which emergency you are facing depends heavily on the child's age — but neonatal conditions can still present later.

GroupConditionsRemember
Neonate (first 28 days)Malrotation / midgut volvulus · hypertrophic pyloric stenosis · Hirschsprung disease · esophageal atresia · anorectal malformationsCan also present later in childhood
Older childrenIntussusception · acute appendicitisAppendicitis = most common pediatric surgical emergency
  • 12-year-old girl after appendectomy for perforated appendicitis — commonest long-term complication → adhesive bowel obstruction. 432 ×2 426

Acute appendicitis

  • Most common cause of acute surgical abdomen in children and adolescents
  • Peak incidence 10-12 years
  • Increased rate of perforation in children
Notes

Acute Appendicitis

The most common pediatric surgical emergency — the danger is delay, especially in young or nonverbal children.

Appendix- Anatomy

  • 6-9cm long, worm-shaped, blind-ending tube.
  • Arise from posterio-medial aspect of the cecum.
  • The base of the appendix is found at the point of convergence of the three taeniae coli of the caecum.
Notes

Overview & Pathophysiology

Most common pediatric surgical emergency; peak incidence 10–12 years, but possible at any age.
Higher perforation rate in children — young / nonverbal patients can't communicate pain → delayed diagnosis and presentation.
Appendix: worm-shaped, blind-ending tube arising from the posteromedial cecum; position is variable — find it where the taeniae coli converge.
Luminal obstruction·Inflammation
Perforation (if untreated)

Acute appendicitis

  • Causes- unclear
  • Path: obstruction of the lumen (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia, foreign body, tumor, parasite)

History

  • Diffuse/periumbilical pain, which eventually localizes to the right lower quadrant
  • Pain followed by nausea/vomiting
  • Anorexia
  • Fever
  • Peritonitis pain: worse with movement, walking (jumping test)
Notes

Clinical Presentation

HistoryExamination
• Periumbilical pain migrating to the RLQ
• Nausea, vomiting, anorexia (loss of appetite), ± fever
• Peritoneal irritation → pain worse with movement		• Unwell, lying still to avoid pain; ± tachycardia (pain / dehydration)
• RLQ tenderness / rebound tenderness — the classic finding
• Rovsing sign: LLQ palpation produces RLQ pain
PEDIATRIC PEARL
Ask the child to jump — refusal to jump because of pain is a useful sign of peritoneal irritation.
DANGER SIGN
Diffuse peritonitis is a bad sign — it suggests perforation.
  • 10-year-old girl, fever, vomiting, RLQ pain for 2 days, RLQ rebound → acute appendicitis. 437 ×4
  • 10-year-old, RLQ pain, fever, tenderness and guarding, high WBC (no US option) → urgent appendectomy. 427 ×2

P/E

  • Child looks unwell, lying still.
  • Tachycardia may be present.
  • Fever
  • Dehydrated
  • Tenderness/Rebound in the right lower quadrant
  • Rovsing’s sign —tenderness in the right lower quadrant elicited when pressure is exerted in the left lower quadrant.
  • Diffuse peritonitis may indicate perforation of the appendix

DDX

  • Appendicitis
  • Gastroenteritis
  • Ovarian torsion
  • Urinary tract infection
  • Mesenteric lymphadentitis
Notes

Differential Diagnosis

Gastroenteritis
Urinary tract infection
Ovarian torsion (particularly females)
Mesenteric lymphadenitis — the classic appendicitis mimic

Investigations

  • Elevated WBC (mainly neutrophils)
  • Urinalysis to exclude UTI
  • Imaging:
    • Not always needed if the diagnosis is clear
    • >6mm, Dilated, thick, hyperemic appendix with adjacent inflammation
    • U/S:
      • Good first line
      • No radiation hazards
      • May miss the appendix
    • CT scan:
      • Very accurate
      • Radiation hazard
  • 10-year-old, RLQ pain, fever, vomiting, guarding, 38.5 °C, high WBC, clear urine → next step confirm with abdominal US. 429 ×2
Notes

Investigations

TestWhat it showsStrengths / limits
CBCLeukocytosisSupportive only
UrinalysisExcludes UTIRules out a mimic
Ultrasound first-lineDiameter >7 mm · hyperemia (↑ blood flow) · inflamed surrounding fat · periappendiceal fluidFast, no radiation; operator-dependent — the appendix may not be visualized
CT with IV contrastClearer visualizationOnly if ultrasound is inconclusive; less operator-dependent, but radiation → minimize in children
LECTURE PEARL — IMAGE EVEN WHEN IT LOOKS CLASSIC
History and exam both point to appendicitis — do you run to theatre? No: order an ultrasound first (quick and easy). Imaging is recommended even with typical findings, to exclude alternative diagnoses.

Acute appendicitis

UltrasoundCT scan

Treatment

  • NPO
  • Intravenous fluid
  • Start antibiotics
  • Urgent Appendectomy (open vs. laparoscopic)
  • Patient can go home next day
  • No antibiotics is required > 24hrs post-operatievely
  • Fast recovery

Ruptured/perforated appendicitis

  • Usually results from delayed presentation/diagnosis/Rx
  • Patient can become very sick (septic shock)
  • Need urgent appendectomy unless abscess cavity has developed
  • Abscess can be treated with antibiotics + percutaneous insertion of drain + interval appendectomy in 6-8 weeks
  • Prolonged recovery
  • Need antibiotics post-operatively
  • High risk of superficial/deep abdominal infections (20%)
Notes

Management

Gold standard: laparoscopic appendectomy. Early appendectomy prevents progression to perforation.

PRE-OPERATIVE BUNDLE
NPO · IV fluids · broad-spectrum antibiotics · patient optimization
Uncomplicated appendicitisPerforated appendicitis
Usual cause—Delayed diagnosis / presentation, particularly young or nonverbal children
ApproachOptimize → laparoscopic appendectomySurgery generally still possible unless presentation is markedly delayed
Presents ≥5 days—Often nonoperative first: IV antibiotics ± ultrasound-guided percutaneous abscess drainage (interventional radiology)
RecoveryUsually discharged the next dayProlonged — often ≥1 week in hospital, then oral antibiotics
Recurrent infection—Risk ≈20%
ANTIBIOTICS ONLY?
Considered when operative / anesthetic risk exceeds the risk of appendicitis — e.g. severe cardiac or respiratory disease.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1

Peak age 10–12 years; perforation is more common in young / nonverbal children because diagnosis is delayed.

2

3

Classic story: periumbilical pain → RLQ with anorexia, nausea and vomiting; exam shows RLQ rebound and Rovsing sign.

Ultrasound first (>7 mm, hyperemia, fat inflammation, fluid); CT only if US is inconclusive — and image even when the picture is classic.

4

Laparoscopic appendectomy is the gold standard; perforation presenting ≥5 days → IV antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage first.

Slide: "imaging not always needed if the diagnosis is clear". Doctor in the lecture: order an ultrasound even when the picture is classic, and the 429 exam key agrees (US before appendectomy) — follow the doctor. If US isn't among the options, a clinically obvious appendicitis goes for appendectomy. Size cut-off: the slide (and standard criteria) say > 6 mm; the notes wrote > 7 mm — use 6 mm.

Malrotation/midgut volvulus

Notes

Malrotation & Midgut Volvulus

LECTURER FOCUS

Bilious vomiting in any child is a surgical emergency — malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.

  • Neonate with bilious vomiting in the first 24 hours, no meconium yet, distension → malrotation with midgut volvulus (the emergency to exclude first). 441

Intestinal rotation

  • Normal rotation of the intestine requires transformation from a simple, straight alimentary tube into the mature fixed and folded configuration normally present at birth.

Normal Rotation

  • Normal midgut rotation:
    • 4-12 weeks of fetal life.
    • 270 counterclockwise movement of the midgut

Malrotation

What is the problem with malrotation?

  • Ladd’s band obstructing the duodenum>>bilious vomiting
  • Midgut volvulus (twisting)>> ischemia and bowel gangrene
  • If not identified quickly>> patient will die due to septic shock
  • If the patient does not die>> entire bowel loss (short bowel syndrome)- not compatible with life
Added explanationIn malrotation the caecum fails to reach the RLQ and usually lies high — in the right upper quadrant / epigastrium — with Ladd's bands running from it across the duodenum to the right abdominal wall.
Notes

Embryology & Pathophysiology

Normal development (weeks 4–12): the bowel temporarily exits the abdomen, rotates 270° counterclockwise, then returns. Normally the ascending and descending colon are fixed retroperitoneally, while the transverse and sigmoid colon remain mobile.

FeatureNormalMalrotation
RotationComplete 270° counterclockwiseAnything other than 270° → abnormal rotation / fixation
Small bowelDuodenum crosses the midline; DJ junction left of the spinePredominantly right-sided
ColonCecum in the RLQ; ascending / descending colon fixedPredominantly left-sided
Mesenteric baseBroadNarrow → predisposes to volvulus
Peritoneal bands FROM NARROW MESENTERY TO GANGRENE—Ladd bands → duodenal obstruction → bilious (green) vomiting
Narrow mesenteric base→Midgut volvulus — twist around mesenteric vessels→Vascular compromise→Ischemia →·Gangrene
IF VOLVULUS IS LEFT UNTREATED
Septic shock, multiorgan failure, death
Extensive bowel loss → short bowel syndrome → severe malabsorption → possible need for intestinal transplantation

Presentation

  • 75% present in the first month of life
  • 15% in the first year
  • Cardinal symptom:
    • BILIOUS VOMITING
  • Other symptoms:
    • Abdominal pain
    • Abdominal wall erythema
    • Distended abdomen (late)
    • Rectal blood (not always )

P/E

  • Lethargic
  • Dehydrated
  • Tachycardia, hypotension, +/- fever
  • Distended upper abdomen (stomach)
  • Distended abdomen (late)
  • Peritonitis (late)
  • Abdominal wall erythema (late)
Notes

Clinical Presentation

≈75% present in the first month of life
+≈15% in year 1
later

Age at presentation of malrotation — ≈90% present within the first year.

NEVER FORGET
Bilious (green) vomiting = a surgical emergency in any child. Keep this in mind for the rest of your career.
Presenting symptomsLate findings — ischemia / necrosisExamination
• Bilious vomiting
• Abdominal pain
• Upper abdominal distension
• Abdominal wall edema / erythema		• Generalized abdominal distension
• Rectal bleeding		• Lethargy, dehydration
• Tachycardia, hypotension
• Abdominal distension
• ± Peritonitis

Investigation

  • Abdominal X ray:
    • Can be totally normal
    • Dilated stomach
  • Abdominal Ultrasound:
    • Reversal SMA SMV orientation
  • Upper GI contrast study:
    • The most sensitive test to diagnose Malrotation (gold standard)
    • Takes time (should not be done if the patient has picture of bowel ischemia)
  • 1-month-old, bilious vomiting, irritable, haemodynamically unstable, X-ray = high obstruction → next imaging → contrast upper GI study (if he is unstable with ischaemia, go straight to laparotomy). 442 ×2
Notes

Investigations

ModalityRole and findings
Abdominal X-rayMay show a dilated stomach — but can be completely normal. A normal film does not exclude malrotation / volvulus.
UltrasoundAssesses SMA / SMV orientation; operator-dependent. (SMV normally lies to the right of the

SMA; reversal or a “whirlpoolˮ twist suggests malrotation / volvulus.) BEYOND NOTES

Upper GI contrast

GOLD STANDARD

Oral / NG water-soluble contrast (e.g. Gastrografin) traces the GI anatomy. Water-soluble is preferred over barium when perforation is possible (risk of barium peritonitis).

CT
Generally avoided in neonates.
DON'T TRUST THE PLAIN FILM
A normal abdominal X-ray never rules out malrotation or volvulus — if the child has bilious vomiting, keep going.
Upper GI studyNormalAbnormal
Duodenal C-loopCrosses the midlineFails to cross the midline; contrast remains on the right
DJ junction / ligament of TreitzLeft of the spine, approximately level with the pylorusAnywhere else = abnormal
Volvulus—Corkscrew appearance
Added explanationOn ultrasound the SMV normally lies to the right of the SMA; reversal, or a "whirlpool" twist of the mesenteric vessels, suggests malrotation/volvulus.

Treatment

Added explanationThe commonest long-term complication after any laparotomy/appendectomy — especially for perforation — is adhesive small-bowel obstruction. Infertility after perforated appendicitis in girls is debated and much less common.
Notes

Management — a Surgical Emergency

Immediate resuscitation: NPO · IV fluids · NG decompression · broad-spectrum antibiotics
Emergency laparotomy + Ladd procedure

THE LADD PROCEDURE, STEP BY STEP

#StepWhy
1Detorse the bowelRestore perfusion
2Resect nonviable bowel, if presentRemove gangrenous bowel
3Divide Ladd bandsRelieve the duodenal obstruction
4Widen the mesenteric baseReduce the risk of recurrent volvulus
5Place small bowel on the right, large bowel on the leftLeaves the gut in the nonrotation position
6AppendectomyPrevents future diagnostic confusion from the abnormal appendix position
WHY THE APPENDECTOMY?
The large bowel — and the appendix — end up on the left, so a future appendicitis would not give classic RLQ pain. It is done to avoid diagnostic confusion, not to prevent recurrent volvulus.
COST OF DELAY
Irreversible bowel gangrene · short bowel syndrome · septic shock · multiorgan failure · death.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1

2

Normal gut rotates 270° counterclockwise (weeks 4–12); anything else = malrotation → narrow mesenteric base + Ladd bands.

Ladd bands → duodenal obstruction → bilious vomiting; narrow base → volvulus → ischemia → gangrene.

3

Bilious vomiting in any child = surgical emergency; ≈75% present in month 1, ≈90% by 1 year.

4

5

A normal X-ray does not exclude it; upper GI contrast is the gold standard — normal DJ junction is left of the spine, level with the pylorus.

Ladd procedure: detorse → resect dead bowel → divide bands → widen base → small bowel right / colon left → appendectomy (for diagnosis, not recurrence).

Ladd’s procedure

  • 3-month-old with malrotation → open surgery (Ladd's procedure by laparotomy). 439

Delayed diagnosis/management

  • Bowel gangrene
  • Short bowel syndrome
  • Septic shock
  • Multi-organ failure
  • Death
Notes

Intussusception

Telescoping bowel in a toddler — bouts of colicky screaming with calm (even sleeping) intervals.

Intussusception

  • Part of the intestine telescopes into the distal bowel by peristaltic activity.
  • Bowel is compressed > venous obstruction > bowel wall edema> arterial insufficiency > ischemia & bowel wall necrosis
  • Causes:
    • idiopathic -95% (Peyer’s Patch)
    • Pathologic lead point- 4% Meckle diverticulum
      • Polyp
      • Neoplasm
      • Inverted appendix
      • Celiac disease, CF, HSP
      • Feeding tubes (GJ tube)
Notes

Definition & Pathophysiology

Telescoping of one bowel segment into another. In children it is most commonly ileocolic / ileocecal — the ileum telescopes into the cecum — though it can occur anywhere in the GI tract.

Telescoped segments compress each other→Venous obstruction→Bowel wall edema→Arterial insufficiency→Ischemia / necrosis
Notes

Etiology

Idiopathic — the usual casePathological lead point
MechanismHypertrophied lymphoid tissue (Peyer patches) in the terminal ileumLead point + peristalsis → bowel telescopes
ContextOften after a viral / upper respiratory infection ~2 weeks earlierPolyps, neoplasms, inverted appendix, Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis), celiac disease, feeding tubes
ClueTypical age group (3 months – 3 years)Recurrent episodes

Presentation

  • Typical age: 3 months-3 yrs
  • Episodic colicky abdominal pain
  • Child is well between the attacks
  • Bilious vomiting
  • Red currant jelly stool
  • Sausage-shaped abdominal mass in RUQ (65% of cases)
  • Empty RLQ
  • 18-month-old, 6 h of episodic crying, legs pulled up, upper abdominal mass → best imaging abdominal ultrasound. 438 ×5
  • 1-year-old, intermittent pain with hip flexion, distension, red currant jelly stool, RUQ mass, target sign → initial management contrast enema. 439 ×5
Notes

Clinical Presentation

Typical age: 3 months – 3 years.

FeatureWhat you see
PainIntermittent, severe, colicky abdominal pain — crying, drawing knees to abdomen; symptom-free and comfortable between attacks, sometimes sleeping
VomitingBilious — due to bowel obstruction
StoolRed currant jelly stool — dark blood mixed with mucus / stool; the classic finding
ExaminationPalpable abdominal mass — the telescoped bowel
  • 18-month-old, URTI a week ago, colicky crying with legs drawn up, mass, blood and mucus PR — most common site → ileocolic. 438
  • 2-year-old, 6 h of episodic crying, unwell, tachycardic, blood with mucus PR, US target sign → intussusception. 442 ×7

Intussusception

AXR: RUQ mass, dilated bowel, Air/fluid levelsUS: gold standard, target sign
Notes

Investigations

TestFinding
Abdominal X- rayDilated loops / air–fluid levels from obstruction — nonspecific
Ultrasound GOLD STANDARDTarget / doughnut sign — concentric layers of invaginated bowel

Management

  • NPO
  • IVF
Reduction enema: under fluoroscopic guidance (done by a radiologist)Surgical reduction: if enema reduction is not successful or not available

IVFReduction enema: under fluoroscopic

Doctor: recurrence ≈ 20%. Book: about 10% after enema reduction (lower after surgery). Use the doctor's figure for his questions.
Notes

Management

Resuscitate: NPO · IV fluids · antibiotics→Therapeutic enema — first line→Surgical reduction if enema fails / unavailable→Resection ± temporary stoma if nonreducible / necrotic
THERAPEUTIC ENEMA — TECHNIQUE
Air, contrast or saline, depending on availability.
Rectal catheter with an adequate seal; gradual, controlled pressure pushes the telescoped bowel back into position.
Careful technique to avoid bowel perforation.
Success: reflux of contrast / air into the small bowel.
Surgical optionWhen
Manual reductionEnema fails or is unavailable — laparoscopic or open
Resection + anastomosisNonreducible or necrotic bowel
Temporary stoma / colostomySevere cases
SKIP THE ENEMA — GO TO SURGERY BEYOND NOTES
Enema reduction is contraindicated with peritonitis, perforation (free air) or shock / hemodynamic instability.
Added explanationSkip the enema — go to surgery when there is peritonitis, perforation (free air) or shock / haemodynamic instability.
Notes

Recurrence

RECURRENCE RULES
Can recur, particularly in the first 24–48 hours; lecture estimate ≈20%.
Recurrent episodes suggest a pathological lead point rather than idiopathic disease.
>3 episodes → operative exploration to find the underlying cause.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1

Ileocolic telescoping at 3 months – 3 years, usually idiopathic (Peyer patch hypertrophy after a viral illness).

2

Recognize it: colicky pain with calm intervals, red currant jelly stool, palpable mass, bilious vomiting.

3

Ultrasound target / doughnut sign is the gold standard; the X-ray is nonspecific.

4

Enema reduction first-line → surgical reduction if it fails → resection if necrotic.

5

Recurrence (esp. 24–48 h) → think pathological lead point; >3 episodes → explore.

Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis

  • Gastric outlet obstruction due to hypertrophied pyloric muscle
Notes

Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis

A hungry baby who can feed but cannot empty the stomach.

  • Classic triad:
    • Term baby
    • 2-8 weeks of life
    • Projectile, non-bilious vomiting
  • 6-week-old, projectile non-bilious vomiting labelled GERD, no response to ranitidine, now dehydrated, X-ray unremarkable → pyloric stenosis. 434 ×2
Notes

Definition & Epidemiology

AspectKey facts
LesionHypertrophy of the pyloric muscle → gastric outlet obstruction
WhoPredominantly full-term infants; males > females
WhenTypically 4–8 weeks of life
Pyloric muscle hypertrophy→Gastric outlet obstruction→Projectile non- bilious vomiting→Dehydration + loss of gastric acid→Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis

Projectile vomiting

Hypertrophic Pyloric stenosis

Hungry & dehydrated baby,

Palpable pyloric muscle (Olive sign)

Gastric peristalsis can sometimes be seen

Electrolytes + blood gas:

Hypochloremia

Hypokalemia

Metabolic alkalosis

Notes

Clinical Presentation

The baby can feed but can't empty the stomach → persistent vomiting.
Projectile, non-bilious vomiting — obstruction is proximal to bile entry. The classic finding.
Infant remains hungry after vomiting but becomes dehydrated from persistent losses.
Palpable olive-shaped pyloric mass; visible gastric peristaltic waves through the abdominal wall may occur.
VERY IMPORTANT — THE CLASSIC BIOCHEMISTRY
Hypochloremic, hypokalemic, metabolic alkalosis
LabChangeWhy BEYOND NOTES
Chloride↓ HypochloremiaCl⁻ lost as HCl in vomitus
pH / HCO₃⁻↑ Metabolic alkalosisH⁺ lost as HCl in vomitus
Potassium↓ HypokalemiaVolume depletion → aldosterone → renal K⁺ loss
  • 4-week-old, non-bilious projectile vomiting after every feed, hungry, mildly dehydrated → best initial imaging abdominal ultrasound. 442
  • Imaging:
    • US: gold standard
    • Thick and elongated pyloric muscle
  • Management:
    • NPO
    • IVF
    • Correct electrolytes and pH
    • Surgical separation of pyloric muscles (pyloromyotomy)
  • Pyloric stenosis — best management → pyloromyotomy (after resuscitation). 439 ×4
Notes

Diagnosis

Gold standard: ultrasound → elongated, thickened pyloric muscle. Clinical history and examination support the diagnosis. Specific ultrasound measurements are not required for this lecture.

Notes

Management

RESUSCITATE ALWAYS BEFORE SURGERY
NPO · IV fluids · correct dehydration, electrolyte disturbances and the alkalosis · NG decompression if needed. Pyloric stenosis is not a reason to rush to theatre.
Resuscitate & correct electrolytes / alkalosis
→Pyloromyotomy — laparoscopic or open→Saline / air leak test
PyloromyotomyDetail
IncisionLongitudinal division of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle without entering the mucosa
Resection?No bowel resection needed
Safety checkIntra-operative saline / air leak test to exclude mucosal perforation
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1

4–8-week-old full-term boy with projectile, non-bilious vomiting who is still hungry → pyloric stenosis.

2

Olive-shaped mass ± visible peristaltic waves; ultrasound (elongated, thickened pylorus) is the gold standard.

3

Know the labs cold: hypochloremic, hypokalemic, metabolic alkalosis.

4

Resuscitate first, then pyloromyotomy — muscle split, mucosa intact, leak test, no resection.

Pyloromyotomy

Esophageal atresia (with or without tracheoesophageal fistula)

Notes

Esophageal Atresia ± Tracheoesophageal Fistula

The drooling newborn whose NG tube won't pass.

  • Interruption in the continuity of the esophagus with or without fistula
  • Caused by error in separation of esophagus & trachea (4th week gestation)
  • 1:4500 live birth
  • Male > female
  • 50-60% associated anomalies
    • VACTERL: Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, TracheoEsophageal, Renal, Limb
Notes

Definition & Embryology

Term / factDetail
Esophageal atresia (EA)Congenital discontinuity — a blind-ending esophagus
Tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF)Abnormal esophagus–trachea connection
EmbryologyFailure of normal separation of the respiratory and GI tracts around week 4 of gestation
Incidence≈1 in 4,500 live births; males more commonly affected
Associations50–60% have other congenital anomalies, particularly VACTERL
Notes

Types

Gas in abdomen?
TypeAnatomyBEYOND NOTESNote
AIsolated EA — no fistulaAbsent (gasless)—
BEA + proximal TEFAbsent—
CProximal blind pouch + distal esophagus communicating with the tracheaPresentMost common
DEA + both proximal and distal TEFPresent—
EIsolated H-type TEF — esophagus continuousPresentFistula causes aspiration
  • Infant with bowel obstruction, X-ray: enlarged gastric gas bubble, no distal bowel gas — where is the caecum? → RUQ. 439
Added explanationGas in the abdomen on X-ray means a distal fistula (types C, D, E); a gasless abdomen means no distal fistula (types A, B).
Notes

VACTERL Association

LetterSystemScreening
VVertebralSpine X-ray ± neonatal spinal ultrasound
AAnalScreen for anorectal malformations
CCardiacEchocardiography
TETracheoesophagealCheck esophageal patency / TEF
RRenalRenal ultrasound, electrolytes, urine output
LLimbSkeletal examination / survey for upper and lower limb abnormalities
RULE
One VACTERL anomaly → screen for all the others.

Presentation

  • Prenatal:
    • Polyhydramnios
  • Postnatal:
    • Drooling
    • Vomiting
    • Respiratory distress
    • Resistance upon insertion of NGT (coiled in the chest)
Notes

Clinical Presentation & Diagnosis

TimingFeatures
PrenatalPolyhydramnios — impaired fetal swallowing of amniotic fluid
Postnatal• Excessive drooling / salivation — inability to swallow
• Vomiting / regurgitation with feeding
• Respiratory distress from aspiration
• Failure to pass an NG tube into the stomach — it coils in the proximal pouch / chest
HOW THE DIAGNOSIS IS MADE
Primarily by failure of NG tube passage, supported by imaging showing the tube coiled in the upper pouch — the classic diagnostic finding. On the same film, gas below the diaphragm means a distal fistula is present.
BEYOND NOTES

Management

  • Urgent surgery
  • Right thoracotomy
  • Division of fistula
  • Repair esophagus
Notes

Management

StepDetail
Definitive repairRight thoracotomy: divide / ligate the TEF (if present) + anastomose the esophageal ends
While awaiting surgeryContinuous suction of the upper pouch (Replogle tube) and head-up positioning to

BEYOND NOTES

limit aspiration

Added explanationWhile awaiting surgery: continuous suction of the upper pouch (Replogle tube) and head-up positioning to limit aspiration.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1

EA = blind-ending esophagus; TEF = esophagus–trachea connection; failure of separation around week 4.

2

Type C — proximal blind pouch + distal TEF — is the most common.

3

Polyhydramnios before birth; drooling, regurgitation with feeds and respiratory distress after.

4

NG tube fails to pass and coils in the pouch — the classic diagnostic finding.

5

50–60% have associated anomalies → full VACTERL screen; repair via right thoracotomy.

Imperforate anusAno-Rectal Malformation (ARM)

Notes

Anorectal Malformations (ARM)

Inspect every newborn perineum — then give the fistula ~24 hours to declare itself.

Imperforate anus

  • Various forms of anorectal anomaly
  • Normal anus:
    • Normal size
    • Location at the center of the muscle sphincter
  • 1:4000
  • Male> female
  • 65% has associated anomalies (VACTERL)
Notes

Definition & Epidemiology

ARM: congenital abnormality of anal / rectal development or position — the preferred term over “imperforate anusˮ.
Normal anus: approximately midway between the coccyx and the scrotal base (males) or vulva (females) — any other position is abnormal.
Incidence ≈1 in 4,000 live births; males more commonly affected.
≈65% have associated VACTERL anomalies → perform full screening.
Notes

Classification

FemalesMales
Perineal fistula — both sexesPerineal fistula — both sexes
Rectovestibular fistulaRectourethral fistula
Cloaca — single opening for urethra, vagina and rectumRectovesical fistula — connection to the bladder
Imperforate anus without fistula — both sexesImperforate anus without fistula — both sexes
Rectal atresia — both sexesRectal atresia — both sexes
Notes

Assessment & Investigations

Inspect the perineum: anal opening? its location? meconium?→Wait ≈24 h for fistula / meconium to appear→Prone cross-table lateral X-ray (invertogram)
Where meconium showsFinding
FemalesMay exit through the vestibule / vaginal region
MalesMay appear on the perineal / scrotal skin, or communicate with the urinary tract
EitherSubcutaneous meconium can produce visible beading along a fistulous track
PRONE CROSS-TABLE LATERAL RADIOGRAPH (INVERTOGRAM)
Mark the expected anus position on the skin, then assess the distance to the distal rectal gas.
MANAGEMENT — GAP IN YOUR NOTES BEYOND NOTES · CHECK AGAINST YOUR LECTURE
The pasted ARM section breaks off here (the text that follows is Hirschsprung material, used in that section). Standard approach for orientation:
Visible perineal fistula (either sex) → anoplasty in the newborn period, no colostomy.
No fistula after 24 h: rectal gas <1 cm from the skin marker → primary posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP); >1 cm → colostomy first, PSARP later.
Rectourethral / rectovesical fistula or cloaca → colostomy first, staged reconstruction.
Added explanationVisible perineal fistula (either sex) → anoplasty in the newborn period, no colostomy. No fistula after 24 h: rectal gas < 1 cm from the marker → primary PSARP; > 1 cm → colostomy first, PSARP later. Rectourethral/rectovesical fistula or cloaca → colostomy, staged repair.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1

“ARMˮ is the preferred term; the normal anus sits midway between coccyx and scrotum / vulva.

2

Females: perineal, rectovestibular, cloaca. Males: perineal, rectourethral, rectovesical. Both: no fistula, rectal atresia.

3

  • Absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric & submucosal plexus of the intestine
  • Arrest in ganglion cells migration from proximal to distal part of GI tract

Notes

Hirschsprung Disease

No ganglion cells, no relaxation — a narrow distal segment with dilated, stool-filled bowel above it.

Notes

Definition & Pathophysiology

Congenital absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the enteric plexuses — submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) → impaired peristalsis and bowel relaxation → functional intestinal obstruction.
Ganglion cells normally migrate proximal → distal; migration stops prematurely → the bowel distal to that point is aganglionic.
Most common site: rectosigmoid junction; may involve other colonic segments or, rarely, the small bowel.

anus

Ganglion-cell migration stops early→Distal aganglionic bowel stays contracted, can't relax→Functional obstruction→Stool accumulates → proximal bowel dilates

Presentation

  • 3-year-old with constipation — the feature pointing to a surgical cause → delayed passage of meconium > 48 h after birth. 434 ×2
Notes

Clinical Presentation

Neonatal presentation — most commonDelayed presentation — short-segment disease
• Delayed passage of meconium — normally passed within 24 hours; failure is an important warning sign
• Vomiting — contents accumulate proximal to the obstruction
• Abdominal distension — dilated, stool-filled bowel
• Feeding intolerance with vomiting after feeds		• Intermittent / incomplete stool passage → often mislabelled “chronic constipationˮ
• Chronic constipation with incomplete emptying
• Marked abdominal distension
• Failure to thrive — thin, wasted extremities with a hugely distended abdomen
• Extreme colonic dilation — lecture case: 12-year-old, cecum ≈20 cm, full of stool
Most patients are diagnosed in the neonatal period, but delayed childhood presentations occur.
LIFE-THREATENING COMPLICATION BEYOND NOTES
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis — fever, abdominal distension and explosive, foul-smelling diarrhea; can occur before or after surgery and can progress to sepsis.
Added explanationHirschsprung-associated enterocolitis — fever, distension and explosive, foul-smelling diarrhoea; before or after surgery; can progress to sepsis. The explosive gush of gas and stool after rectal examination is a classic sign.
  • 3-week-old, 2 weeks of distension, needs anal stimulation to pass stool, explosive foul gas/feces on PR, no rectal air → Hirschsprung disease. 437 ×6

Diagnosis

  • Rectal manometry: absent recto-anal inhibitory reflex.
  • Contrast study.
  • Rectal biopsy:
    • Gold standard
    • Look for ganglion cells in the myenteric & submucosal plexus

TRANSITION ZONE
The change from narrow distal to dilated proximal bowel — it marks the boundary of aganglionosis. The dilated bowel above it is normally ganglionated; it expands only because of retained stool.
  • One-day-old who hasn't passed meconium (Hirschsprung) — how to investigate → contrast (barium) enema, then rectal suction biopsy to confirm. 441

Treatment

  • Resection of aganglionic bowel
  • Pull through procedure
Notes

Treatment

Definitive treatment: resection of the aganglionic bowel + pull-through of normally ganglionated bowel, anastomosed to the anus — usually laparoscopic(-assisted). Surgery is required to definitively relieve the functional obstruction.

Identify the aganglionic segment→Intra-op biopsies → pathology confirms ganglionated level→Resect the aganglionic segment→Pull normal bowel down through the anus→Anastomose bowel to anus

Postoperative Follow-Up

FOLLOW UP INTO ADULTHOOD (≈18 YEARS)
Bowel-related complications may persist — regular pediatric surgical follow-up is needed, as with other surgically treated congenital GI conditions. Watch for:
Constipation
Anastomotic stricture
Bowel-function problems needing an ongoing regimen
Other postoperative complications
